tagline.text: World Heritage terraces fanning out on both sides of a river in Kiangan

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (green fields in June–July)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~1,500 (per person, based on local transport and snacks in Kiangan; guide and entrance fees to be confirmed locally)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL; overland from Manila to Lagawe and Kiangan)

children.text: Nagacadan is one of the five UNESCO World Heritage rice terrace villages in Ifugao, located in Kiangan. It is an open-air museum village where you walk among terraces and homes rising in rows on both sides of a river and learn about Ifugao rice culture.

The Nagacadan Rice Terraces are in Nagacadan village, in the municipality of Kiangan, Ifugao province, deep in the Cordillera range of northern Luzon. In 1995 UNESCO inscribed the five Ifugao terrace villages (Batad, Bangaan, Hungduan, Mayoyao Central and Nagacadan) together as the Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras (reference 722). It was the first property inscribed worldwide in the cultural landscape category, and it was recognized under cultural criteria (iii), (iv) and (v). Wikipedia describes the Nagacadan terraces in Kiangan as two rows of terraces rising on either side of a river. Simply remember the shape of terraces climbing like a fan up both slopes with a river down the middle.

There are several stories about the age of the Ifugao terraces. The UNESCO listing describes them as more than 2,000 years old, but research by the Ifugao Archaeological Project, which Wikipedia cites, suggests the terraces at their present scale were built about 400 years ago, shortly after Spanish contact. Some accounts say terraces were first used for growing taro and that rice replaced it around 1600. With scholars disagreeing like this, the exact age is hard to settle. What is clear is that the skills for building the terraces and managing the water were handed down orally without written records, and that harvests, rituals and songs have been passed along together.

What sets Nagacadan apart from other terrace villages is its character as an "open-air museum." The Nagacadan Open Air Museum is a community-based project that the Kiangan local government began together with the FAO's Globally Important Agricultural Heritage Systems (GIAHS) project, and the village community runs it directly. Income from visitors is said to go to museum upkeep, repairs of terraces and irrigation channels, festivals and traditional ceremonies. In other words, instead of entering a museum building you walk along paddy banks, forest paths and through the village to see the life of the Ifugao people itself. Along the route there are several traditional houses and granaries, and the path crosses a river and passes between the fields.

This guide is for travelers who have already been to Banaue and Batad, or who want to see Ifugao quietly away from the crowds. Kiangan is the old center of Ifugao; it served as the provincial capital through the Spanish, American and Japanese periods until the capital moved to Lagawe in 1949. The road to the village is not difficult, so if you arrange a guide and schedule in advance you can visit within half a day. Information on fees and opening hours was too thin to write here, so be sure to confirm with the Kiangan tourism office. Checking the latest notices is the most important habit in a place like this.

blocks.title: Terraces rising in rows on both sides of a river

children.text: The Nagacadan fields climb the slope in two rows with a river between them. Each paddy is built up in stone-walled steps, and village houses sit among the fields, so the whole scene looks like a single painting. From just after planting through June–July the fields are green and most popular, and before harvest they turn golden.

blocks.title: Walking the Nagacadan Open Air Museum

children.text: Along the path through fields, forest, village and river stand several traditional houses and granaries. The museum was created to show Ifugao culture in a way that does not disturb daily life, and local guides explain the history along the way. Walking time depends on your guide and plan, so discuss it with the Kiangan tourism office.

The hudhud is an epic chant sung by Ifugao women while harvesting rice. The museum program is described as letting you hear hudhud at harvest time. Schedules vary with season and village circumstances, so ask in advance.

The life of the Ifugao is tied to the rice cycle, and rituals accompany each planting and harvest. At the museum a guide explains the meaning of these rituals. Some rituals are held on set dates, so whether you can see them depends on when you visit.

blocks.title: A look inside a traditional house

children.text: Along the museum path there are several traditional houses and granaries, and the museum program is described as letting you enter a traditional house to see how the Ifugao live. Ask your guide about the rules on shoes and photography before you go in.

The museum offers activities such as tying rice bundles for storage and carving a bulul, the Ifugao ceremonial figure. The activities and prices may change, so ask the Kiangan tourism office before you visit.
A trek of about
6 hours

is described that crosses the mountains from Nagacadan through Maggok to Hungduan. You can stay overnight in Maggok, and Hungduan has spider-web-shaped terraces and homestays. Decide carefully, weighing your fitness, the weather and safety.

blocks.title: The Yamashita surrender site and the Ifugao Museum

children.text: In Kiangan town stands the Kiangan Shrine, which marks the place where General Tomoyuki Yamashita of the Japanese army surrendered on September 2, 1945. The Ifugao Museum stands in the same area, and local guidance says it displays Ifugao artifacts. Its opening hours and fees have not been confirmed, so check locally.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: Kiangan town and the Nagacadan museum

children.text: Stop at the tourism office behind the municipal hall in Kiangan, announce your visit and be assigned a guide.
Ride a tricycle to Nagacadan. It is described as taking about 10 minutes from Kiangan.
Walk the paddy banks and forest path with your guide and look at the traditional houses and granaries.
Listen to the hudhud chant or an explanation of the rice rituals, and try tying rice bundles or carving a bulul.
Return to Kiangan town for lunch and see the Yamashita surrender shrine and the Ifugao Museum.
Time varies greatly with your guide and activities. The museum is run by the village community, so contact them in advance to confirm the schedule.
Prepare for departure at the Nagacadan museum and enter the mountain trail with your guide.
Discuss with your guide whether to rest in Maggok village or stay the night.
Arrive in Hungduan, look at the spider-web-shaped terraces and rest at a homestay.
The jeepney from Hungduan to Banaue is said to leave at 10 a.m. A tricycle is about ₱400~500.
This route is based on a blog account. Safety and trail conditions can change greatly, so be sure to consult a local guide.

items.title: From Manila to Lagawe and Kiangan

children.text: According to Wikipedia, Kiangan is about
355 km
from Manila. I could not confirm a direct scheduled service, so look up the overnight bus timetables toward Ifugao (to Banaue) and ask the conductor whether you can get off at Lagawe.
The Ohayami bus to Banaue from the Sampaloc area of Manila is quoted by different sources at about ₱470~740, and the trip takes about 9 to 10 hours. Fares may have risen, so confirm when you book.
Buses fill up on holidays and weekends, so book ahead.
Kiangan is about
10 km
from Lagawe, the Ifugao provincial capital. Jeepneys are described as running about once every two hours, and tricycles are also available.
The fare has not been confirmed, so check locally.
From central Kiangan to the Nagacadan Open Air Museum is about
10 minutes
by tricycle. The method described is to meet a guide at the tourism office behind the municipal hall and travel together.
Letting them know of your visit in advance is said to help with preparations. The Kiangan local government's contact (kianganlgu@yahoo.com) is given.
From Banaue you travel to Kiangan via Lagawe. Direct public transport may be limited, so ask your lodging or the tourism office how to get there.
The jeepney from Hungduan to Banaue is said to leave at 10 a.m., and a tricycle is about ₱400~500.

Kiangan is a highland area ranging from about 416 to 1,477 m above sea level, averaging about 841 m. Mean daily highs are about 21–25 degrees and lows about 14–19 degrees, so it is cool. Annual rainfall is about 2,835 mm over about 238 rainy days a year, so rain is frequent.

Rain is heaviest from June to August and lightest in January. Guides also say the fields are greenest in June–July and harvest continues around August, but schedules differ by village, so ask your guide. The dry season of November–May is comfortable for walking, but from January to March the fields are bare and the scenery can look plain.

I could not confirm specific lodging information for Kiangan town and the village area. Visiting for the day from a place in Kiangan or Lagawe is the simplest approach. If you take the mountain trek, you can also stay overnight at a homestay in Maggok or Hungduan, so ask your guide. For Banaue, see
Banaue Rice Terraces

Eating at restaurants in Kiangan town is the usual choice, and since I could not confirm specific restaurants, ask the tourism office for recommendations. There is a notice that Banaue has no banks or ATMs, and this region relies heavily on cash, so bring plenty of cash and keep in mind that mobile signal is weak in places.
Contact the Kiangan tourism office before your visit to book a guide and schedule.
Always go with a guide, who will point out dangerous sections of the paddy paths and local etiquette.
Paddy banks are narrow and slippery, so bring non-slip shoes and trekking poles.
Bring water, snacks and a rain jacket. Kiangan has many rainy days.
Ask permission before photographing people or their homes.
Do not step into the fields or on the channels and stone walls. Repairing a collapsed wall takes great effort.
Bring plenty of cash. Banks and ATMs may not be nearby.
If you plan to see Banaue and Batad too, leave generous travel time.
This is a village where people live. Do not step on the fields, damage the stone walls or take photos without permission, and follow the museum program and your guide.
I could not confirm entrance fees, opening hours or activity prices. Check with the Kiangan tourism office before your visit.
Paddy banks and mountain paths are very slippery in the rain. Postpone your trip on heavily rainy days.
The trek over the mountains to Hungduan takes about 6 hours, so check your fitness and the weather and go with a guide.
Ifugao is a mountainous region at risk of earthquakes, typhoons and landslides. Avoid traveling when weather warnings are in effect.
The transport and fare information here is based on blog and wiki accounts and may have changed. Check the latest notices.
